must_remember: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is caused by an unusually short eyeball along its optical axis or insufficient converging power of the cornea-lens system.
The near point of a hypermetropic eye recedes from the standard reference distance of $25\text{ cm}$ to a greater distance $D'$.
A convex (converging) lens is used to correct hypermetropia by forming a virtual image of a near object at the patient's shifted near point.
The focal length ($f$) and optical power ($P$) of the corrective convex lens are always positive.
When a spectacle lens is worn at a distance $d$ from the cornea, the effective object and image distances must account for this gap: $u = -25\text{ cm}$ and $v = -(D' - d)$.

glossary.meaning: An eye defect where distant objects are seen clearly, but near objects are blurred because images focus behind the retina.
The closest point to the eye at which an object can be brought into sharp focus by accommodation; shifted outward in hypermetropia.
The degree of convergence or divergence of a lens, measured in diopters (D), equal to the reciprocal of focal length in meters ($P = 1/f$).
A converging lens thicker at the center than at the edges, used to add positive dioptric power for hypermetropia correction.
